title: 12/19/2025 | Dallas County Public Works | COM | Dallas County Public Works Comments on Implementation of SB 6

documents.text:
=== Dallas County Public Works Comments SB6 Implementation_1.docx ===
Protecting Local Ratepayers
Dallas County Public Works supports economic development associated with Data Centers.  However, the costs associated with upgrading transmission lines and substations for "Large Loads" (75 MW+) should not be subsidized by existing residents.
The "Fair Share" Argument: The PUCT should strictly enforce the SB 6 provision that requires Large Load customers to pay for their own interconnection costs.
Preventing Stranded Costs: Dallas County Public Works has concerns about "ghost loads"—companies that reserve capacity but never actually build. Dallas County Public Works advocates for high, non-refundable security deposits.  This will prevent over-building of infrastructure that local residents might eventually be forced to pay for through higher rates.
Mandatory Curtailment for Non-Critical Loads
Dallas County Public Works supports the PUCT’s draft rule requiring new large industrial customers to have remote-disconnect technology.
Residential Priority: In an emergency, "firm load shed" events (similar to Winter Storm Uri), large data centers and crypto miners should be the first to be disconnected to keep the lights on in residential neighborhoods and for critical services and facilities (hospitals, water treatment).
Verification: Dallas County Public Works requests that ERCOT perform annual testing of these curtailment protocols to ensure they work during a real grid emergency.
Lowering the "Large Load" Threshold
While SB 6 sets a default threshold of 75 MW, Dallas County Public Works supports the PUCT staff’s recommendation to lower this to 25 MW.
Local Impact: In a dense urban area like Dallas, even a 25–50 MW facility can significantly strain a local distribution substation. Lowering the threshold ensures more of these projects are subject to the heightened planning and financial standards of SB 6.
Transmission Planning and "4CP" Reform
Dallas County Public Works supports the reform of the Four Coincident Peak (4CP) methodology.
The Issue: Currently, many large industrial loads "dodge" transmission costs by lowering their usage for a few hours during summer peaks.
The Comment: This places an unfair burden on residential consumers who cannot easily shift their load. Dallas County Public Works supports a new cost-allocation model that reflects total grid usage, ensuring Large Loads contribute more to the multi-billion-dollar transmission upgrades currently underway in North Texas.
Protecting County and State Roadways
Dallas County Public Works supports protection of County roads and Infrastructure 
Section 37.101 states that a municipality may require an electric utility to relocate the utility’s facility at the utility’s expense to permit the widening or straightening of a street – this should be extended to County governments and to the State to protect infrastructure in general.  
The large loads for the interconnection is damaging County roadways and Farm-to Market Roads significantly Therefore, County governments should be allowed to require deposits or cost recovery fees for permits associated with Large Load interconnection.
